## Why this unit matters

- **Sensitivity:** which inputs move a chosen output?
- **Identifiability:** which parameters can the observation process distinguish?
- A narrow optimizer interval is not evidence that every biological parameter is learned.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes, and set the shape of the session: three tools, one question each.
Local sensitivity asks what happens if I nudge a parameter. Global sensitivity
asks which parameter is responsible for the spread in outcomes across a whole
plausible range. Structural identifiability asks a different kind of question
altogether: not what the model does, but what the data could ever tell us about
it.

Keep one distinction visible all session, because everything here turns on it:
perturbing a model is not the same as learning from data. This is also the last
slot of a long day, so promise the payoff early. The session ends by proving
something about this afternoon's reporting fraction.
:::

## Baseline SIR model

Deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state, population model:

$$
\dot S=-\beta cSI/N,\qquad
\dot I=\beta cSI/N-\gamma I,\qquad
\dot R=\gamma I.
$$

At the course baseline,
$N=1000$, $(S,I,R)=(990,10,0)$,
$(\beta,c,\gamma)=(0.05,10,0.25)$, and
$\mathcal R_0=\beta c/\gamma=2$.

The state sensitivity matrix is
$J_x(t)=\partial x(t)/\partial(\beta,c,\gamma)$.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Same baseline as every other session, so nothing here is new except
the notation for the sensitivity matrix.

Plant one seed and move on: beta and c never appear apart in these equations,
only as the product beta-c. Ask the room what that might mean for estimating them
separately, take one answer, and say the last part of the session settles it.

One warning about the parameterisation: from here the code uses a positional
vector [beta, c, gamma] rather than the named tuple of the earlier sessions,
because the sensitivity and Sobol APIs index parameters by position. The
worksheet flags this too.
:::

## Local sensitivity: a derivative, not an uncertainty interval

For a small perturbation,

$$
\Delta z\approx\nabla_\theta z\,\Delta\theta.
$$

Raw derivatives carry the units of their own parameter: since the model uses
only $k=\beta c$, $\partial I/\partial\beta=c\,\partial I/\partial k$ and
$\partial I/\partial c=\beta\,\partial I/\partial k$, a factor $c/\beta=200$
apart wherever they are nonzero. The elasticity
$(\theta_j/I)\,\partial I/\partial\theta_j$ is dimensionless and comparable
across parameters.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-slide-ch10-local
#| fig-cap: "Centered local derivatives of infectious prevalence, raw and as dimensionless elasticities."
using CairoMakie
using EpiModelingCourse
using OrdinaryDiffEq

const N10 = BASELINE_PARAMETERS.N
const u010 = [BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.S, BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.I,
    BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.R]
function sir10!(du, u, p, t)
    β, c, γ = p
    incidence = β * c * u[1] * u[2] / N10
    du[1] = -incidence
    du[2] = incidence - γ * u[2]
    du[3] = γ * u[2]
end

times10 = collect(0.0:1.0:40.0)
p010 = [0.05, 10.0, 0.25]
# Differencing two trajectories cancels most of the signal, so the solves need
# tighter tolerances than the trajectories themselves would.
solve10(p) = Array(solve(ODEProblem(sir10!, u010, (0.0, 40.0), p),
    Tsit5(); saveat = times10, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10))
base10 = solve10(p010)
local10 = Matrix{Float64}(undef, length(times10), 3)
for j in 1:3
    δ = 1e-5 * p010[j]
    plus = copy(p010); plus[j] += δ
    minus = copy(p010); minus[j] -= δ
    local10[:, j] = (solve10(plus)[2, :] .- solve10(minus)[2, :]) ./ (2δ)
end
fig10 = Figure(size = (980, 380))
ax10 = Axis(fig10[1, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "∂I/∂θⱼ",
    title = "Raw: unit-dependent")
ax10e = Axis(fig10[1, 2], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "(θⱼ/I) ∂I/∂θⱼ",
    title = "Elasticities: dimensionless")
for (j, label) in enumerate(["β", "c", "γ"])
    style = j == 2 ? :dash : :solid
    lines!(ax10, times10, local10[:, j], label = label, linestyle = style)
    lines!(ax10e, times10, p010[j] .* local10[:, j] ./ base10[2, :],
        label = label, linestyle = style)
end
axislegend(ax10e)
fig10
```

::: {.notes}
Eight minutes, and the curves are worth reading aloud rather than summarising.
Each one is the derivative of infectious prevalence with respect to one
parameter, over time. They start at zero, since at day zero nothing has happened
yet, peak around the epidemic peak, and change sign afterwards, because raising
transmission moves the epidemic *earlier* as well as higher, so late in the
window a bigger beta means fewer people still infectious.

Read the left panel first and let the room fall into the trap. Beta looks
overwhelming and c looks like a flat line at zero. Ask whether that means beta
matters more, then spring it: the two curves differ by exactly two hundred,
which is c over beta. Beta is measured per contact and c in contacts per day, so
the derivatives are in different units and the comparison is meaningless. Nudging
beta by 0.01 is a twenty percent change; nudging c by 0.01 is nothing at all.

The right panel divides that out, asking instead for the percentage change in I
per percentage change in each parameter. Now beta and c lie exactly on top of
each other, which is why c is dashed — otherwise it would be invisible. That
coincidence is the session in one picture: nothing in this plot could tell the
two apart, and Worksheet Part A has them verify it numerically.

Two warnings. This is a derivative at one parameter vector, so it says nothing
about behaviour a long way from the baseline; that is the next slide. And a
derivative is not an uncertainty interval and not a posterior; a large derivative
means a parameter matters, not that we know it badly.
:::

## Global variation: sharing out the variance

Vary all three parameters across a plausible box and ask how much of the
*variance* in peak prevalence each one accounts for:

- $S_1$: the share that parameter explains **on its own**.
- $S_T$: its share **including every interaction** it takes part in.

$S_T > S_1$ means the parameter matters in combination with others;
$\sum_i S_1^i < 1$ is the part of the variance no single parameter owns.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-slide-ch10-global
#| fig-cap: "One-at-a-time swings and Sobol indices over the same parameter box."
using GlobalSensitivity
using Logging

function peak10(p)
    sol = solve(ODEProblem(sir10!, u010, (0.0, 40.0), Float64.(p)),
        Tsit5(); abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8)
    # Dense interpolation on a sub-daily grid, since the peak falls between days.
    maximum(sol(t)[2] for t in 0.0:0.05:40.0)
end

boxes10 = [[0.02, 0.08], [5.0, 15.0], [0.15, 0.40]]
oat10 = [peak10([j == k ? boxes10[j][2] : p010[j] for j in 1:3]) -
    peak10([j == k ? boxes10[j][1] : p010[j] for j in 1:3]) for k in 1:3]

Logging.disable_logging(Logging.Warn)
sobol10 = gsa(peak10, Sobol(), boxes10; samples = 500)
Logging.disable_logging(Logging.BelowMinLevel)

fig10g = Figure(size = (980, 350))
ax10a = Axis(fig10g[1, 1], xticks = (1:3, ["β", "c", "γ"]),
    ylabel = "change in peak I", title = "One at a time")
barplot!(ax10a, 1:3, oat10; color = :grey65)
ax10b = Axis(fig10g[1, 2], xticks = (1:3, ["β", "c", "γ"]),
    ylabel = "share of variance", title = "All three at once (Sobol)")
barplot!(ax10b, (1:3) .- 0.18, sobol10.S1; width = 0.34, color = :steelblue,
    label = "first order, alone")
barplot!(ax10b, (1:3) .+ 0.18, sobol10.ST; width = 0.34, color = :darkorange,
    label = "total, with interactions")
ylims!(ax10b, 0, 0.6)
axislegend(ax10b; position = :lt)
fig10g
```

::: {.notes}
Ten minutes, and it is the heart of the session. Walk the left panel first: move
one parameter from the bottom of its range to the top, holding the others at
baseline, and record the swing. It gives a ranking, and it is what most people do
by hand. Then say what it cannot see: it never leaves the baseline for the other
two parameters, so a parameter that only matters when transmission is already
high looks unimportant.

The right panel varies all three together. Point at the gap between the blue and
orange bars: that gap is interaction. Here the first-order shares sum to roughly
0.85 — nearer 0.89 on a far larger design — so of the order of a tenth of the
variance belongs to no parameter individually. Both panels depend entirely on
the box; widen the bounds and the
ranking can change, which is the caveat to state out loud.

One caveat that the next slide will sharpen. Beta and c get separate bars here
only because we sampled them as two independent uniforms, and the sizes of those
bars follow from the two boxes we chose, not from anything the model
distinguishes. Sobol answers which input ranges drive the spread in the output;
it never answers which parameters could be estimated. Anyone reading a taller
beta bar as "we can measure beta" has confused the two questions, which is
exactly what the observation map settles next.

Two footnotes if asked. The package warns that its design matrices are not fully
independent QMC sequences; that is suppressed here for legibility and does not
change the picture at this sample size. And 500 samples is deliberate: the
worksheet repeats this at 32 and shows the indices are unstable, even negative,
when the sample is too small.
:::

## The observation map

Only incidence is observed:

$$
y(t)=\beta c\,S(t)I(t)/N.
$$

The transformation $(\beta,c)\mapsto(a\beta,c/a)$ leaves this map unchanged.
Thus $\beta$ and $c$ are structurally confounded; $\beta c$ can be learned.

The reporting fraction $\rho$ from the previous session is the same argument with
a twist: observing $\rho C(t)$, the pair $(\rho,\beta c)$ is confounded **only if
the initial state is unknown**. Treat $S(0), I(0), R(0), C(0)$ as known and both
become identifiable. Background knowledge, not more data, is what buys it.

::: {.notes}
Eight minutes. This is the payoff for the observation-models session, so name the
callback explicitly: this afternoon we said a small epidemic fully reported and a
large one partly reported look alike, and here is the precise version.

Be accurate about the twist, because it is the interesting part. Scaling the
whole population up and the reporting fraction down leaves the observed counts
unchanged, so with unknown initial conditions only the ratio survives. Declaring
the initial state breaks that symmetry, and the worksheet runs both cases and
gets exactly that. Say "the initial state", not "the population size": the
worksheet marks all four initial values known, which is a stronger assumption
than knowing $N$ alone. The lesson is that
identifiability is a property of the model *plus* what you already know, not of
the equations alone.

Contrast with the beta-c case above, which no amount of external knowledge about
population size repairs. There you need contact data or an independently
measured c.
:::

## API and validation

The derivatives above came from finite differences. The library computes them
directly, by solving the variational equations alongside the model:

```{julia}
#| label: ch10-forward-sensitivity
using SciMLSensitivity

local_problem = ODEForwardSensitivityProblem(sir10!, u010, (0.0, 40.0), p010)
local_solution = solve(local_problem, Tsit5(); saveat = 0.0:1.0:40.0)
states, jacobians = extract_local_sensitivities(local_solution, true)

# One Jacobian ∂(S, I, R)/∂(β, c, γ) per saved time; row 2, column 1 is ∂I/∂β.
forward = [jacobian[2, 1] for jacobian in jacobians]
finite_difference = local10[:, 1]
agreement = maximum(abs.(forward .- finite_difference)) /
    maximum(abs.(finite_difference))
(; saved_times = length(jacobians),
   relative_difference = round(agreement; sigdigits = 2))
```

- `SciMLSensitivity`: forward sensitivities or adjoints.
- `GlobalSensitivity`: Sobol first-order and total indices.
- `StructuralIdentifiability`: `assess_identifiability`, run in the worksheet.
- Validate: check $S+I+R=N$, and one derivative two ways, as above.

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. The point of running this live is that the augmented problem and
the finite differences agree to about one part in ten thousand, so the earlier
plot was not an artefact of the perturbation size, and you now have the API that
scales to models where finite differences would be hopeless.

Worth one aside if the room is with you: that agreement needs tight solver
tolerances on both slides. A centered difference subtracts two trajectories that
differ in the fifth decimal place, so at the default tolerances the same
comparison only agrees to a couple of percent, and the error is in the finite
difference, not in the library. That is the practical argument for the
variational equations even when a finite difference is available.

The one API not executed here is `assess_identifiability`: it compiles for tens
of seconds on a cold session, which is not something to do in front of an
audience. That is why it lives in the worksheet, and why the warm-up cell during
the break matters. Say that out loud rather than skipping past it.
:::

## Takeaways and limitations

- Local: neighborhood behavior around one parameter vector.
- Global: ranking conditional on ranges and a design.
- Structural: information available in an idealized observation map, and in
  what you already know, such as the initial state.
- Practical identifiability also depends on noise, sampling, initial states, and misspecification.

Read the [book chapter](../../chapters/11-sensitivity-and-identifiability.html)
for derivations and exercises; see the
[SciMLSensitivity](https://docs.sciml.ai/SciMLSensitivity/stable/),
[GlobalSensitivity](https://docs.sciml.ai/GlobalSensitivity/stable/), and
[StructuralIdentifiability](https://docs.sciml.ai/StructuralIdentifiability/stable/)
documentation for APIs.

::: {.notes}
Four minutes, and it is the last thing anyone hears on Day 2, so land it rather
than reading the bullets.

Ask which of the session's conclusions are about the model and which are about
the data. The Sobol ranking is about the model and the box we chose; the
identifiability results are about the data and what we already know. Confusing
the two is how people end up reporting a confident estimate of a quantity their
data never contained.

Then hand over to tomorrow: sensitivity tells you which parameter to spend effort
on, and the intervention session asks what to do about it. Flag that
Part C of the worksheet is where the reporting-fraction result gets proved, and
that the two inference chapters it points at are self-study, not sessions here.
:::
